newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swissair CFO says forecasts to be reduced.
newsitem.headline: Swissair CFO says forecasts to be reduced.

text.p: Georges Schorderet, chief financial officer of Swissair AG, said the airline's expectations for full-year results will be reduced downward slightly due to lower-than-expected traffic figures.
Georges Schorderet, chief financial officer, also said that analysts' forecasts for net profit between 150 and 200 million Swiss francs were in the high end.
"We will report a positive result for the full year, but our expectations will be reduced slightly based on today's view," Schorderet told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"We had higher expectations for traffic figures," Schorderet added, noting that a one percent swing in seat load factor had a 40 million franc impact on the bottom line.
Swissair reported a first half group net loss of 51 million Swiss franc, down from 86 million the year before.
In 1995 the airline group reported a 1995 net loss of 147 million francs, but this was largely due to extraordinary restructuring costs of 340 million.

Airline business, however, is very seasonal and analyst Roland Leutenegger at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), for example, expects Swissair to report a full year net profit of 174 million Swiss francs.

Schorderet said flight operations in the first half had not reached the company's target, but the deficit was still smaller than last year. He declined to specify the first half loss in flight operations.
The unit cost in flight opearations was reduced by seven percent, but this was countered by a five percent drop in yield, Swissair said earlier.
Schordered said around one-fourth of the five percent yield decline, or between 1.0 and 1.5 percent, was due to currencies with the rest accounted for by continued price erosion.

Swissair expects yields to continue to decline by around five percent in the medium term, partially due to the continuing price erosion in the industry, but also as Swissair continues to adjust its prices downward.
"Our prices are still above our competitors, but over time we will lose our price advantage," Schorderet said.

Asked whether Swissair's targets for flight operations remained on track, Schorderet said the aim was unchanged and the company still wanted to achieve a return on invested capital of 12 percent by 1998.
"I don't see any other way," he said.
A lot of the cost-cutting measures that Swissair is undertaking will start to bite in 1997.
"You should not forget that Swissair is a practically a construction site," he said.
Since March Swissair has launched a series of projects to reduce costs, such the optimisation of work flow and processes, and personnel reduction.
Schorderet also said purchasing would be reviewed in order to try to save costs, but the company would still not reduce the quality of the Swissair product.
"But must we always buy the most expensive?" Schorderet said.

Swissair's first half revenue rose 10.7 percent, substantially more than expected by analysts, but much of this rise was due to recent acquisitions, including duty-free businesses in Australia, Schorderet said.
The duty-free activities of Britain's Allders Plc, which Swissair acquired earlier this year, were not consolidated in the first half.
-- Peter Nielsen, Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
